resolutions.researcher_notes: Wikipedia's 'Transcontinental Pipeline' article infobox states 'est = 1950' — exact match for StartYear1=1950. Confirmed via the article's raw wikitext (fetched action=raw) that this infobox field carries no inline footnote of its own (it is supported only by the trailing categories 'Energy infrastructure completed in 1950' / '1950 establishments in New York'), and that the article's only two inline citations (a FERC pipeline-code list, and an EPA settlement page) are unrelated to the founding date and are NOT gem.wiki or any GEM surface — so this is a clean, GEM-free single source. Single source only (no second independent publisher found stating 1950), so tier is capped at medium and independent:false per the brief's rubric. Extensive search for a second corroborating source (Williams' own FY2018 and FY2025 10-Ks, williams.com/pipeline/transco/ fact page, FERC pipeline docket materials via elibrary.ferc.gov) turned up narrative descriptions of Transco's history/geography but no other document stating an explicit in-service/founding year of 1950; elibrary.ferc.gov is not fetchable in this environment (returns an empty Angular JS shell regardless of URL pattern tried).

Could not find any source stating the sheet's exact system-wide Main Line design capacity of 16,800 MMcf/d. Checked: (1) Williams' FY2025 joint 10-K (wmb-20251231.htm, CIK 99250/107263) and FY2018 10-K (wmb_20181231x10k.htm) — both describe Transco's geography and note expansion projects' incremental capacities (e.g. specific project Dth/d figures) but state no single system-wide 'Main Line' capacity number; (2) williams.com/pipeline/transco/ (fetched live, 200 OK) — its 'Operational Details' fact card gives 'System Peak Design Capacity: 19.5 million dekatherms per day' (~19,500 MMcf/d) and 'Miles of Transmission Pipeline: 10,000' and '60' compressor stations — none of these figures matches the sheet's 16,800 MMcf/d, 10,200 km, or any exact figure, and this fact card appears to describe the FULL Transco system (all laterals) rather than the 'Main Line' segment the sheet row is scoped to, so it is not proposable as a supporting match; (3) EIA's FERC-Form-61-derived 'EIA-StatetoStateCapacity_Jan2026.xlsx' workbook (Pipeline State2State Capacity tab) lists Transco's individual state-to-state border-crossing capacities for every year 1990-2025 — the single largest crossing in the most recent year (2025) is 5,118 MMcf/d (Alabama-Georgia) and no crossing or straightforward combination of crossings sums cleanly to 16,800 MMcf/d, so this dataset neither confirms nor is directly citable for a whole-system total (it measures point-to-point capacity, not a rolled-up system design capacity, and combining crossings into a system total would be original synthesis, not a citation); (4) Wikipedia's infobox gives 'discharge = 3.5 trillion cu ft per annum' (~9.59 Bcf/d average annual throughput) — a different metric (average annual throughput vs. design/peak capacity) that does not match 16,800 MMcf/d and was not proposed. FERC eLibrary (would likely hold the original certificate/expansion orders stating design capacity) is not fetchable in this environment. CONCERN: none of the company's own current materials describe a whole-system capacity anywhere near 16,800 MMcf/d as a single figure — the two figures actually found on Williams' own site (19,500 MMcf/d peak design capacity, full system) and the largest single EIA border crossing (5,118 MMcf/d) bound the true figure loosely but do not corroborate 16,800 specifically. This may reflect the sheet value being an older/point-in-time design-capacity figure for the Main Line segment specifically, which none of the sources checked isolate.

Could not find a source matching the sheet's 10,200 km (~6,340 mi) Main-Line-specific length. The two length figures found both describe the FULL Transco system (not the Main Line segment alone) and both disagree with the sheet: Wikipedia's infobox states 'length_mi = 10500' (10,500 mi = 16,900 km), and Williams' own website fact card (williams.com/pipeline/transco/) states 'Miles of Transmission Pipeline: 10,000' (10,000 mi = 16,090 km). Both whole-system figures cluster near 10,000-10,500 miles, roughly 60% longer than the sheet's 10,200 km (6,340 mi) value — consistent with a genuine scope difference (GEM's row is explicitly labelled 'SYSTEM/NETWORK INFO (Main Line)', i.e. the trunk only, excluding laterals/branches, while both found sources describe the entire system including laterals), so neither is proposed as a supporting ref for this Main-Line-specific figure (would be an orphan/non-matching ref). Checked Williams' FY2018 and FY2025 10-Ks for a Main-Line-only mileage statement — neither gives a specific mileage figure for Transco at all (narrative geographic description only). FERC eLibrary (likely holder of the original certificate documents describing Main Line-only mileage) is not fetchable in this environment. CONCERN: flagging for Update review — it is possible the sheet's 10,200 km value itself reflects a unit or scope mislabel (e.g., a Main-Line-only sub-total, or km/mi conflation, given 10,200 in miles would be 16,415 km, close to Wikipedia's 16,900 km whole-system figure) but this is speculation not confirmed by any source; not changing the value per instructions.
